Sahyadri Systems: Prioritising Under Constraints

Pune, India — Friday, 18 September 2026

1. The Friday before the freeze

At half past three on 18 September 2026, Ananya Deshpande stood at the whiteboard on the fourth floor of Sahyadri Systems' Baner office in Pune, looking at a backlog she had rewritten four times that week. In ninety minutes she was due in the quarterly roadmap-freeze meeting, where the October–December sprint plan would be locked and handed to Karthik Iyer's team in Bengaluru for sprint-zero planning on Monday. Once locked, nothing moved without a formal change request and a fight. Ananya, Sahyadri's Vice President of Product, had budgeted six weeks to make this call carefully; she had four days, because the ground under the plan had shifted three times since August: a regulator had moved a deadline, a marquee customer in Dubai had escalated, and a data-integrity bug had turned into a legal letter from a fleet owner in Kolhapur. Whatever she wrote on that whiteboard by 5 p.m. would decide which of four capable, opinionated colleagues — spread across Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey — spent the next thirteen weeks unhappy.

2. Sahyadri Systems

Founded in 2016 by two IIT Bombay classmates, Sahyadri Systems began as a maker of ruggedised GPS trackers for long-haul trucks. By 2019, fleet owners were asking less for a tracker and more for answers — where is my truck, why is this trip late, what did this driver actually do — and the company rebuilt itself around a cloud platform called TrackSetu, sold as hardware-plus-software to logistics and trucking fleets. By the September 2026 quarter, TrackSetu was fitted to roughly 58,000 vehicles across 340 fleet accounts, ranging from large third-party logistics operators to owner-operators with a dozen trucks, generating annual recurring revenue of about ₹34 crore. Sahyadri competed against Locus and FarEye on routing and visibility, and against Shipsy and in-house fleet systems on analytics; its pitch was hardware and software a dispatcher could actually use, at a price a mid-sized transporter could afford. Like every logistics-tech vendor in India, TrackSetu's invoicing was wired into the GST e-way bill system and, for toll reconciliation, into FASTag data — plumbing invisible to customers until it broke, answering to deadlines Sahyadri did not set.

3. The situation

Three things had converged on the same quarter. First, in early September, GSTN notified transporters that the e-way bill API would move to a new authentication version from 1 October, old version switched off — not optional, and squarely Sahyadri's problem since TrackSetu auto-generated e-way bills. Karthik had already committed two of his six product engineers to the migration for six weeks. Second, Sahyadri's largest single account, Gulf Horizon Logistics, a Dubai-based freight operator worth ₹4.2 crore in annual recurring revenue — roughly one-eighth of company ARR — had told Marcus Lim, Sahyadri's Singapore-based customer-success lead for Gulf and Southeast Asian accounts, that its board would decide at renewal, timed around Diwali, whether to stay with TrackSetu or move to FarEye, unless Sahyadri shipped a custom geofencing and driver-behaviour-scoring module promised since March. Third, and closest to home, a GPS-drift defect logged as low-priority for two quarters had produced a distance-billing dispute with Konkan Roadlines, a Kolhapur-based transporter whose owner sent a lawyer's notice disputing ₹18 lakh in trip charges, warning he would raise the matter with other fleet-owner associations. Karthik's engineers found the same drift, at smaller scale, in thirty-seven other mid-market accounts.

From where each of them sat, the picture looked different. Karthik, watching his roadmap from Bengaluru, saw a team that could not physically do everything being asked of it. Marcus, watching a renewal clock from Singapore, saw the company's biggest account walking toward the door. Devika Rao, Sahyadri's Toronto-based data scientist, saw a competitor's conference talk about predictive maintenance and worried a quarter's delay would cost Sahyadri a story it had spent a year building. And Bill Kessler, running enterprise sales from New Jersey, saw a further ₹6 crore of Gulf-region pipeline waiting to see how Gulf Horizon's renewal went before anyone else signed.

4. The people

  • Karthik Iyer — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. Owns the finite pool of engineers and the compliance deadline he cannot move. Wants a plan he can commit to without silently overrunning it, and wants the GPS-drift defect treated as an engineering-integrity problem, not a customer-relations inconvenience.
  • Marcus Lim — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Manages the Gulf Horizon relationship personally and has told its operations director a fix is "in the next release." Wants the geofencing module built at full scope before Diwali, and fears that anything less reads as Sahyadri deprioritising its biggest customer.
  • Bill Kessler — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Is forecasting ₹6 crore of new Gulf-region ARR on the strength of Gulf Horizon's renewal as a reference. Wants Ananya to protect the account that protects his pipeline, and is wary of engineering time going to a bug that, in his view, "nobody outside Kolhapur has heard of."
  • Devika Rao — Data Scientist, Toronto. Has spent five months building a predictive-maintenance model and believes it is the product's next real differentiator against Locus and FarEye. Wants a firm slot in the quarter, not another "next time," and worries the model's business case erodes the longer it waits.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 lays out the four discretionary backlog items competing for engineering time, scored the way Ananya's team normally scores a backlog — Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort — with the e-way bill migration shown separately because it is not really a backlog item at all; it is a fixed cost the quarter must absorb before anything else is scheduled.

Read mechanically, Exhibit 1 ranks the GPS-drift fix first, the UI redesign second, predictive maintenance third, and buries Gulf Horizon's feature last — 0.24 against 102 for the bug fix — because Reach counts accounts, not revenue, and one account is one account whether it is worth ₹40,000 or ₹4.2 crore. That is the classic failure of a mechanical score once a constraint has changed: the inputs no longer describe what is actually at stake, and Ananya cannot hand this table to Marcus or Bill as if it settled anything.

Exhibit 2 makes the problem concrete: the four discretionary items in Exhibit 1 add to 29 engineer-weeks, and only 26 remain once compliance and a support reserve are taken out. Something does not fit — not "everything, slightly late," but one item cut, or all four thinned. It also shows why RICE alone cannot answer this: ₹4.2 crore in one relationship and ₹3.6 crore spread thinly but attached to a legal notice are both real money, and neither is obviously larger once risk, not just revenue, is weighed in.

Exhibit 3 places the quarter's fixed dates against the discretionary decision window Ananya actually controls.

Exhibit 3 — the compliance cutover on 1 October is fixed by GSTN; Gulf Horizon's renewal conversation is effectively fixed around Diwali; only the eight weeks between them are truly Ananya's to allocate without slipping a hard date.

Exhibit 3 shows why this is not simply a ranking exercise: two of the four dates on the line are not Sahyadri's to move — a constraint with a calendar of its own, not a preference to be argued down.

6. The options

Option A — Protect the anchor account

Staff Gulf Horizon's full geofencing and driver-scoring module first, using senior engineers, followed by the UI redesign; push the GPS-drift fix and predictive maintenance entirely to Q4. This secures the ₹4.2 crore renewal and the pipeline behind it, and lets Marcus walk into the renewal talk with a shipped feature, not a promise. Its cost: the drift defect stays live across all 340 accounts, leaving the ₹3.6 crore mid-market segment and Konkan Roadlines' notice unaddressed, and it teaches the organisation that the loudest customer always jumps the queue.

Option B — Fix the foundation first

Use the 26 discretionary weeks to fully fix the GPS-drift defect and ship the predictive-maintenance model, defer Gulf Horizon's module entirely to Q4, and offer a contractual service credit to bridge the gap. This closes a systemic billing-integrity problem before it produces a second notice, and lands the bet Devika believes matches what FarEye is about to announce. Its cost: a real chance of losing Sahyadri's largest account — 12% of ARR — before the credit is proven to hold past Gulf Horizon's Diwali decision, putting Bill's Gulf pipeline at risk.

Option C — Descope and sequence both

Build a minimal Gulf Horizon module — software-defined geofences on existing telemetry, without the driver-behaviour-scoring model — at roughly four engineer-weeks instead of ten; fully fix the GPS-drift defect at six weeks; and explicitly move predictive maintenance and the UI redesign to Q4, with Devika given a two-week discovery spike so her work is not lost. Total: twelve of twenty-six available weeks, leaving buffer against slippage. This closes the billing-trust problem across the base and gives Gulf Horizon something real to renew against, but the module is visibly thinner than a competitor's pitch, and Bill's expansion pipeline depends on how well it lands.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does a strict RICE ranking recommend, and where does it plainly misread what is at stake? What has to be added back into the score by judgment rather than arithmetic?
  2. The e-way bill migration never appears as a scored backlog item, yet it already consumes twelve of the quarter's twenty-six discretionary weeks. How should Ananya treat a constraint that is not a product decision at all when she reprioritises the rest of the plan?
  3. Karthik, Marcus, Bill and Devika each have a legitimate, well-argued claim on the same fixed pool of engineers. In what order, and on what evidence, should Ananya have these conversations so the final call reads as reasoned rather than as whoever spoke to her last?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what, specifically and by what date, would you tell Gulf Horizon's account team and Konkan Roadlines' owner about what happens to their requests?

8. A note for the learner

Prioritising under constraints is not a one-time ranking exercise; it is what happens to a ranking when the ground it was built on moves. Here the ground moved three times in a month: a regulator fixed a date Sahyadri did not choose, a stakeholder's stakes changed the meaning of "impact," and a bug sitting at the bottom of the backlog turned out to carry legal weight the original score never captured. RICE scoring, stakeholder mapping and engineering estimates still apply — Exhibit 1 shows that — but each input must be re-priced against the new constraint, not inherited from last quarter. Effort is scarcer, since twelve weeks just left the pool for a mandate with no score at all. Reach undercounts a revenue-concentrated account, so it cannot be read alone. And a defect's true Impact is not what it looked like when logged, but what it looks like after a lawyer's letter.

A well-reasoned answer does the arithmetic in Exhibit 2 before arguing values — twenty-six weeks against twenty-nine of demand is a forced choice, not a rounding error — and treats the 1 October cutover as fixed, not negotiable. It resists "biggest number wins": ₹4.2 crore in one account and ₹3.6 crore across thirty-eight already in dispute are both consequential, and a strong answer says explicitly why one risk should dominate the other.

The defensible path is Option C. The GPS-drift defect is fixed in full because a billing-accuracy failure is a compounding, portfolio-wide liability that worsens the longer it survives a legal notice, and letting it run tells every fleet owner that disputes are how you get engineering attention. Gulf Horizon gets a real, narrower commitment rather than silence, respecting both the relationship Marcus has built and the limits Karthik works within. Predictive maintenance and the UI redesign move to Q4 on a named date, not a vague "later." Options A and B are not unreasonable, and a class may defend either, provided it argues plainly why one risk should outweigh the other. What separates a strong answer from a weak one is not which option a student picks, but whether the reasoning was rebuilt from this quarter's actual constraints rather than carried over unexamined.

Anubandh Engage: The Winter Cut

Gurugram — Sunday, 15 November 2026, 11.40 p.m.

1. The night before

Meghna Sarin had three windows open on the dining table of her flat in Sector 53, Gurugram, and none of them agreed with the others. The first was the engineering capacity sheet Suhas Kamat had sent from Hyderabad at nine that evening, which said Anubandh Engage had 214 usable engineer-weeks between now and the end of February. The second was the product plan she had defended to the board in August, which assumed 286. The third was an email from Hilal Retail Group's chief information officer in Dubai, sent on a Sunday, asking for a written attestation of tenant data isolation by 15 December and copying two people Meghna had never met.

At nine the next morning she would open the meeting the company had taken to calling the winter cut: forty minutes with engineering, revenue, legal and finance to decide what Anubandh would build between December and February, and, more painfully, what it would stop building. On Friday she would take whatever came out of that room to a board call with Beas Ridge Capital, who had put ₹40 crore into the company in April on terms that included a headcount freeze. Meghna had run this exercise six times since joining as Vice President of Product in 2023, never with a live security disclosure, a sixteen-per-cent revenue concentration, a regulator's clock, a hiring covenant and a pod down three engineers inside the same fortnight.

What unsettled her was not that the list was long. It was that every framing she tried produced a different winner, and she could not tell whether that meant the list was wrong or the framings were.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2021

Anubandh Engage was founded in Gurugram in 2017 by Suhas Kamat and Ritika Vohra, both formerly of a Bengaluru analytics firm, to sell Indian consumer brands something their marketing teams were then buying badly: one place to hold customer data, segment it, and send campaigns across SMS, email, push and, later, WhatsApp. The wager was that India's D2C boom would produce hundreds of brands too small for Adobe or Salesforce and too serious for spreadsheets. It was broadly right. By November 2026 Anubandh carried 231 paying accounts and annual recurring revenue of ₹46.5 crore, with engineering split between Hyderabad's HITEC City and a platform team in Kochi's Infopark, product and revenue in Gurugram, and a handful of senior people scattered across Singapore, Berlin, Toronto and New Jersey.

The decision that shaped everything since was taken in October 2021, when Anubandh had ₹9 crore of ARR and a cash runway of seven months. Hilal Retail Group, a Dubai-based operator of supermarkets and fashion formats across the Gulf, offered a three-year contract worth ₹3.2 crore prepaid on one condition: the platform had to run inside the UAE, on infrastructure Hilal's auditors could inspect, because Hilal's own group policy — and its reading of UAE data rules — would not permit customer records to sit in Mumbai. Ritika, then chief executive, took the money. The engineering consequence was a second deployment, known internally as the Gulf build, running an older infrastructure stack in a Dubai region, with its own release train.

Five years later the Gulf build was nine releases behind the Indian platform, and every feature that touched storage or identity had to be written, tested and certified twice. A 2024 internal study had put the resulting overhead at eighteen per cent of platform engineering time. Nobody had re-measured it since, and Farida Qureshi, who ran the platform team in Kochi, believed it was now closer to a quarter. Hilal had grown into Anubandh's largest account at ₹7.4 crore, or roughly sixteen per cent of ARR, and had never once been asked to move.

3. The industry

Anubandh competed in a crowded Indian category. MoEngage, CleverTap, WebEngage and Netcore Cloud had all raised more money and sold further up-market; Salesforce, Braze and Adobe circled the enterprise accounts. Every Indian brand with a loyalty programme — the Nykaas and Lenskarts and boAts of the market, the quick-commerce players, the large-format retailers — was somebody's logo in a slide. Anubandh's position was the mid-market: brands doing ₹50 crore to ₹700 crore of revenue, who wanted campaign tooling that worked on the first day and a support engineer who answered on WhatsApp.

Three external forces bore directly on the roadmap. The first was TRAI's commercial-communications framework, under which every template and header had to be registered on the telecom DLT registry and scrubbed before delivery; a misfire there was not merely embarrassing but traceable, complaint-generating and expensive, since WhatsApp Business conversations and SMS were billed per send and passed through to the brand. The second was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the rules under it, whose notice, consent-artefact and erasure obligations would bind data processors of Anubandh's class from May 2027 — far enough away to defer, close enough that a platform rewrite could not be started in April. The third was payments: Anubandh's subscription-billing module, sold to D2C brands running replenishment plans, rode on e-mandates and UPI Autopay through a payment-aggregator partnership with Razorpay, and NPCI's revised Autopay parameters required re-certification by 31 January 2027 or the module would simply stop taking new mandates.

Roughly thirty-one per cent of ARR came from outside India: the Gulf, a Singapore-managed Southeast Asian book, and two US brands sold out of New Jersey. That mix was the growth story and most of the complexity.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In March 2026, Meghna's team had scored the annual backlog using the RICE method the company had adopted in 2024 (Exhibit 2). The scoring took four days, involved eleven people, and produced a ranking that the board saw in April and that had governed planning ever since. Its top item was Audience Studio, a self-serve segment-builder with lookalike expansion, shipped to the Indian platform in July. Its second was the Next Best Action engine that Dr Anjali Menon was building in Toronto. Compliance work sat sixth.

On 12 August, a change to the Audience Studio export path went out with a filter scoped to the cluster rather than to the tenant. For twenty-eight days, a lookalike audience built by one brand could, under a particular combination of settings, be seeded with hashed identifiers derived from another brand's data on the same cluster. No raw personal data left any tenant boundary; what crossed it were salted hashes and aggregate counts. The defect was found not by Anubandh but by Nachiket Phadke, an independent security researcher in Nagpur, who emailed a proof-of-concept on 11 September and asked for a response within ninety days.

Engineering confirmed the defect on 18 September and closed it the same night. Establishing who had been affected proved impossible. In 2024, to hold down an infrastructure bill that had grown faster than revenue, the platform team had reduced audit logging on the audience cluster to a ten per cent sample. Anubandh's security lead, reading the sampled logs pessimistically, put the number of tenants whose data might have been drawn on at fourteen. Farida's platform team, reading the same logs and the export-job metadata, said three were confirmed and the remainder were artefacts of sampling. Both readings appear in Exhibit 4, and both were circulated to the executive team in the same week, which is how the company came to hold two official numbers.

Meanwhile the ground moved three more times. On 28 August, three of the seven engineers in Kochi resigned within nine days: two to a global capability centre in Bengaluru at roughly 1.6 times their salary, one to a bank in Dubai. Because of the Beas Ridge covenant, backfilling required a board exception rather than a requisition. On 14 October, at an industry event in Mumbai, two competitors demonstrated agentic campaign orchestration, and Anjali's Slack messages acquired a new urgency. On 4 November, during Charkha Living's Diwali campaign, a throttling defect in the WhatsApp connector re-sent 4.1 lakh messages; Charkha, a ₹1.9 crore home-and-wellness brand out of Jaipur and Anubandh's most quotable Indian reference, was billed about ₹22 lakh for the duplicates and filed a complaint that touched DLT compliance. On 30 October, Hilal's security questionnaire arrived: forty-eight controls, a request for SOC 2 Type II, and the isolation attestation now due 15 December — three weeks before the date on which Hilal's renewal option lapsed.

The assumption that had quietly failed was the one nobody had written down. In March, the team had scored the backlog on the belief that capacity would grow, that the Gulf build's overhead was a known eighteen per cent, and that compliance was configuration. By November, capacity had shrunk, the overhead was contested, and Farida's engineers had concluded that a defensible isolation fix required the per-tenant key separation that the Gulf fork made prohibitively expensive to do twice.

5. The people

Meghna Sarin, VP Product, Gurugram. Owns the winter cut and will present it on Friday. Publicly she says the decision must follow from evidence rather than volume. Privately she has noticed that the March scores are the only numbers anyone trusts, and that she does not trust them. She has not told the board that the plan they approved in April was built on a capacity figure that is now twenty-five per cent too high.

Suhas Kamat, co-founder and CTO, Hyderabad. Argues that the isolation rework is not a feature but a debt that has already come due, and that doing it properly means confronting the Gulf build. His incentive is technical credibility with a team that has watched him defer this twice. What he does not say in meetings is that he took the Hilal money in 2021, and that a rewrite is also an admission.

Farida Qureshi, Head of Platform, Kochi. Down to four engineers from seven, with two notice periods still running. She wants the winter cut to name what will not be done, in writing, because her team has absorbed every unnamed commitment for two years. She has not told Meghna that one of her four remaining engineers has an offer in hand.

Yusuf Rahman, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Manages Hilal and the Southeast Asian book, flies to Dubai monthly, and has told Hilal's CIO that the attestation "will not be a problem." His bonus is tied to gross revenue retention. He has not circulated the part of his September call notes in which Hilal's CIO mentioned that the group had begun a vendor evaluation.

Dr Anjali Menon, Head of Machine Learning, Toronto. Believes Next Best Action is the only item on the list that changes Anubandh's competitive position, and has a pilot showing an eighteen per cent lift (Exhibit 5). Her incentive is a model shipped before the category commoditises. She has not volunteered that the pilot ran without a holdout group, or that two of the four pilot brands were simultaneously running discount campaigns.

Nikhil Sodhi, Chief Revenue Officer, New Jersey. Forecasts ₹11 crore of new ARR for the coming year, of which ₹6.4 crore assumes Hilal renews and acts as a reference in the Gulf. He wants the quarter spent on Hilal and on NBA, which he can sell. He has not told Meghna that two of his three largest US prospects have asked for SOC 2 Type II, which Anubandh does not hold.

Shalini Bakshi, Head of Legal and Privacy, Mumbai. Cannot say with confidence whether salted hashes constitute personal data under the DPDP framework, and therefore cannot say whether the August incident is notifiable. Her position is that the company should behave as though it is. She has not said that the ninety-day window in Nachiket Phadke's email expires on 10 December, and that she has no control over what he publishes afterwards.

Ravi Subramanian, CFO, Gurugram. Reports ₹31 crore in the bank against a monthly burn of ₹2.6 crore, and an ARR covenant of ₹62 crore before the headcount freeze lifts. He is the only person in the room who thinks in rupees per engineer-week rather than in engineer-weeks (Exhibit 1). He has not said that ₹1.1 crore of Hilal's 2021 prepayment remains unearned on the balance sheet and is contractually refundable if certain roadmap commitments go undelivered.

6. Exhibits

Prioritising under constraints

Re-ordering is not re-arguing. The discipline is to find the resource that actually binds, price one unit of it, and make every change to the plan pay that price in public.

1 Two decisions, one week apart

On Monday 9 February 2026, Rohit Barve, vice-president of product at Yashodhan Freight Cloud in Pune, opened a quarter plan that three separate events had made obsolete over the weekend. Yashodhan sells a transport-management platform to Indian freight forwarders and third-party logistics operators — ₹ 96 crore of annual recurring revenue, about sixty engineers across seven squads, and a quarterly planning cadence that had just finished its sixth week.

The first event was a renewal. Yashasvi Retail, a distribution business worth ₹ 8.4 crore a year — 8.75 per cent of Yashodhan's revenue — had made a custom electronic proof-of-delivery workflow a condition of renewing on 30 April, and had simultaneously escalated a rate-engine performance problem that made quoting slow at month-end. The second was regulatory: the e-way bill API used by every Indian goods movement was moving to a new version with a compliance date of 1 June, and the migration had not yet been scheduled. The third was arithmetic Barve had been avoiding. Of the fourteen items sitting in the integrations squad's queue, the average had been waiting thirty-one days; meanwhile two core platform squads were finishing early and picking up cleanup work. Every customer-specific commitment in the company routed through six engineers.

Three days later and a hundred and fifty kilometres away, Tanvi Deshpande faced a structurally different problem at Chhanda Play, a Mumbai consumer app that teaches people to play the harmonium, guitar and tabla by listening to them practise. Chhanda Play had 4.2 million monthly active users and 310,000 subscribers paying ₹ 249 a month. The company's largest marketing spend of the year — a festive campaign with a media commitment already signed — would begin on 14 March. The iOS release train departed fortnightly; the last train that could carry code to users before the campaign left on 5 March, with a code freeze on 28 February. And on 12 February the mobile lead reported a crash regression in the practice recorder affecting roughly six per cent of Android sessions, about 62,000 sessions a day.

Deshpande's constraint was not engineer-days. She had engineers. What she did not have was trains, and no amount of overtime creates one. Barve's constraint was engineer-days, but not the ones he had been counting. Between them the two decisions cover most of what makes this topic hard: the resource that binds is rarely the resource that is measured, and the arithmetic that ranks work correctly also, quietly, prevents you from ever fixing the thing that made the arithmetic necessary.

2 The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

Prioritising under constraints is the practice of deriving a plan from two inputs held deliberately apart: a value ordering over candidate work, and a statement of the scarce resource that limits how much of it can be done. The plan is the ordering with a line drawn where the resource runs out. A constraint is any resource whose exhaustion changes what is feasible — engineer-days, a shared reviewer, a release train, a bill-of-materials cost ceiling, a kilobyte of flash memory, a certification lab's calendar, a regulator's date. A constraint is binding if you would consume more of it were more available; a resource you are not fully using is not a constraint, however scarce it feels.

The formal machinery is post-war operations research. George Dantzig's simplex method (1947) turned resource allocation into linear programming, and with it came duality: attached to every binding constraint is a shadow price, the marginal value of one more unit of that resource. Leonid Kantorovich had reached related results in Leningrad in 1939, work that eventually shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize with Tjalling Koopmans. The discrete cousin, the knapsack problem, supplies the greedy rule that most product backlogs unknowingly implement: sort by value divided by resource consumed, fill from the top. The rule is provably optimal when items are divisible and merely very good when they are not.

Two later traditions translated this into management. Eliyahu Goldratt's The Goal (1984) argued that a system's throughput is set by one bottleneck, so the whole discipline reduces to five steps: identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, and repeat. Donald Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supplied the product-development economics — cost of delay, queueing costs, and the sequencing rule of dividing cost of delay by duration, which SAFe later packaged as Weighted Shortest Job First. RICE, published by Intercom in 2016, is a recipe for the numerator of that ratio and nothing more; treating it as a theory of prioritisation is the single most common category error in the field.

These traditions do not agree, and the disagreements are not semantic. They produce different plans from the same backlog.

3 Mechanics in depth, including what gets left implicit

Expert practice is a sequence of seven moves, of which the first and the last are the ones that distinguish practitioners. The middle five are arithmetic that any competent person can perform.

Find the binding constraint empirically. The evidence is queueing, not utilisation. A resource is binding when work piles up in front of it and waits. Barve's integrations squad had fourteen items with a mean wait of thirty-one days; his core squads had no queue at all. High utilisation on a resource with no queue means the resource is busy, not scarce. The distinction is unintuitive and consequential: teams routinely conclude that engineering is the constraint because engineers are busy, when the real queue is in front of a single security reviewer, a shared data-science team, a device lab, or a fortnightly release train.

Separate the type of change. A capacity change moves the budget line and nothing else; the value estimates are unaffected, and any meeting that reopens them is waste. A customer event changes one or two numerators and may add a pinned date. A defect changes the state of the world: it creates a cost that accrues while you do not act, so its value is a function of delay rather than a constant. Confusing these three is the origin of most long re-planning meetings.

Pin what is not a choice. Regulatory dates, contractual commitments and safety work are constraints in the costume of backlog items. They come off the capacity before sorting begins. Barve's e-way bill migration scores poorly on any value model and must ship anyway; scoring it and then overriding the score is worse than not scoring it, because it teaches the team that the model is decorative.

Express value in one currency and divide. Yashodhan uses annualised contribution in ₹ lakh — new ARR plus probability-weighted retained ARR — divided by engineer-days of the constrained squad. The division is the whole method. Ranking by value rather than value density is the single most common failure among people who use the vocabulary correctly.

Read the shadow price off the cut. The density of the first item that does not fit is the marginal value of one unit of the constraint. This number, not the ordering, is the artefact experts carry around. It converts every future request — an escalation, a favour, a “can we just squeeze in” — from a social negotiation into a priced transaction.

Re-slice before re-scoring. The denominator is a design decision. An item that does not fit may contain a thin slice that captures most of its value at a third of its cost, and slicing frequently moves a candidate from below the line to near the top. Experts attack the denominator first because it is under their control in a way that value estimates are not.

Publish the displacement. Every addition names a subtraction, in writing, to the person who owns the subtracted item. This is the move that converts prioritisation from an internal exercise into an organisational contract, and it is the one most often skipped, because it is the only step that requires telling somebody something they do not want to hear.

The second-order effects that the arithmetic does not contain

Three of these matter enough to change decisions. The first is the constraint-elevation blind spot. Density is computed against the current constraint, which the model holds fixed; therefore any item whose benefit is to relax the constraint is systematically undervalued, because its return arrives as released capacity in future periods rather than as customer value now. Barve's self-serve carrier sandbox is exactly this item, and a naïve density ranking puts it last, permanently.

The second is queueing cost. Delay in a system with variable arrivals and variable service times does not rise linearly with utilisation; it rises hyperbolically. Kingman's approximation gives waiting time as proportional to u/(1 − u) multiplied by a variability term, which means the same team planned to ninety-five per cent of capacity waits roughly five times as long for any given item as one planned to eighty per cent. A plan with no buffer is not an ambitious plan; it is a plan whose delivery date is a lottery.

The third is switching cost. Re-ordering is not free. Partially completed work becomes inventory that ages, context is lost, and every publicised change to a roadmap consumes a small amount of the credibility that makes future commitments possible. The correct conclusion is not that re-ordering is bad but that it has a price which should appear on the same ledger as the density gain it captures.

4 When the method applies, stated as testable claims

Density arithmetic earns its keep under four conditions, each of which can be checked rather than assumed.

Claim one: one resource binds, and you have identified it. Testable by looking for the queue. True for Barve — integrations is the only place work waits — and false for Deshpande, whose engineers are not the scarce thing. Applied to Barve, the method works; applied to Deshpande, ranking her app backlog by engineer-days would produce a beautifully ordered list that has no bearing on what ships before 14 March.

Claim two: items are roughly independent and roughly divisible. Testable by asking how many items have prerequisites among the others, and whether any item is more than about a fifth of total capacity. Barve's ePOD workflow at sixty days against 330 is at the edge; his self-serve sandbox at ninety days is not divisible by the greedy rule's assumptions and must be treated as a lump.

Claim three: value estimates are comparable in a single currency. Testable by asking two people to score the same item independently. Yashodhan's currency — probability-weighted annualised contribution — works because its value is mostly contractual. Chhanda Play's does not translate as cleanly: the value of a retention improvement is a statistical claim about a cohort, and the value of a crash fix is an avoided loss whose size depends on the counterfactual.

Claim four: the ordering is stable to plausible estimate error. Testable directly. Multiply every large estimate by 1.6 — the rough empirical size of the planning-fallacy asymmetry between large and small items — and see whether the set above the line changes. If it does, the plan rests on the estimates rather than on the values, and the honest response is to slice the large items until it does not.

The method is actively misleading in three situations. When the true constraint is a calendar rather than a quantity, density ranks items that cannot be scheduled at all. When value is jointly produced — the two sides of a marketplace, or a feature that only matters if another ships — item-level density is not additive and the arithmetic silently overstates the plan's total. And when the decision is irreversible, density says nothing about the option value of waiting: a forty-day item that can be undone and a forty-day item that commits a tooling order are not the same forty days, though the model treats them identically.

5 Worked example one: the seam, not the queue

Barve's integrations squad had six engineers and, after the support rota and leave, 330 planned engineer-days in the quarter. Exhibit 2 is the queue as he found it on 9 February, with value expressed as annualised contribution in ₹ lakh. The ePOD workflow is scored at ₹ 420 lakh, which is the ₹ 840 lakh Yashasvi Retail renewal multiplied by the account team's fifty per cent estimate of the probability that the renewal turns on this feature — a number Barve disliked and used anyway, on the principle that an explicit weak estimate is easier to argue with than an implicit one.

Run the same exercise on the core platform group — eighteen engineers, 990 planned days — and the marginal item comes in at about ₹ 0.4 lakh per day. The two numbers are the real finding of Barve's Monday. An engineer-day is worth three and a half times more on the integrations squad than on the core platform, which means the most valuable decision available to him is not a better ordering of either list. It is moving capacity across the seam between them.

The constraint-elevation blind spot then shows itself. I9, the self-serve carrier sandbox, ranks last at ₹ 1.3 lakh per day. But its function is to remove integrations work permanently: the squad's own estimate was that self-serve onboarding would take about thirty-five engineer-days per quarter off the queue, or 140 days a year. Valued at the squad's own shadow price of ₹ 1.4 lakh per day, that released capacity is worth about ₹ 196 lakh a year on top of the item's direct value of ₹ 120 lakh. Its true density is therefore (120 + 196) ÷ 90 ≈ ₹ 3.5 lakh per day, which moves it from ninth to fourth. Nothing about the item changed. What changed was whether the model was allowed to notice that the constraint is not a law of nature.

This is precisely where the flow economist and the constraint theorist part company, and both are right about something. The flow economist says: fine, put the released-capacity value in the numerator and let the arithmetic handle it. The constraint theorist says: you will not, because the released value accrues to a future quarter and your planning horizon is this one, so you need a rule rather than a number — reserve capacity for elevation and stop pretending the ranking will get there on its own.

6 Worked example two: when you cannot buy a train

Deshpande's problem does not respond to any of this. Chhanda Play's iOS builds go out fortnightly; the campaign starts 14 March; the last usable train is 5 March with a freeze on 28 February. Her decision variable is not how many engineer-days to allocate but which of four things occupies the sixteen days between 12 and 28 February, given that the mobile squad can realistically land two of them and that the pitch-detection model improvement depends on a shared ML platform team with a five-week queue.

The correct analysis begins by classifying the cost-of-delay shape of each item rather than its magnitude. The onboarding rebuild has a spike-and-collapse shape: it is worth ₹ 1.9 crore if it lands before the campaign and close to nothing afterwards, because the traffic it was built to convert will have come and gone. The pitch-detection improvement has a shallow linear shape: shipping it in April costs roughly a month of the annualised benefit, about ₹ 22 lakh, which is real but not urgent. The crash has a compounding shape: every day it persists adds to a pool of users who have formed a view about the product's reliability, and unlike feature value, that cost does not stop accruing when you finally act.

The plan Deshpande arrived at follows from the shapes. The crash fix goes out as an Android hotfix on 17 February, outside the train, because the compounding shape makes waiting eleven days for the scheduled release the most expensive option on the board — ₹ 3.4 lakh a day for eleven days is ₹ 37 lakh, against five engineer-days of work. The onboarding rebuild takes the 5 March train and is scoped to fit, not estimated to fit: the team agreed on 14 days of appetite and cut the two hardest screens rather than let the item grow. The pitch-detection work is escalated not as a priority but as a queue problem, with a request to the ML platform team for a reserved slot in the following quarter, which is the only intervention that changes anything. And the subscription self-serve work is removed from the conversation entirely, because it has no date and therefore no business competing for a dated resource.

7 Worked example three: the failure, and what recovery cost

Yantrika Devices, a Coimbatore manufacturer of smart prepaid energy meters selling to state distribution utilities, spent most of 2024 running a disciplined prioritisation process against the wrong resource. The product team ranked firmware and application features by value per engineer-week, filled the roadmap, and delivered almost exactly what the plan said. They then lost a tender worth ₹ 61 crore and spent fourteen additional weeks and about ₹ 3.4 crore reworking the design.

The cause was structural. Engineering capacity was not binding. Three other resources were, simultaneously: the bill-of-materials headroom against the price at which the meter could win a tender, the free flash memory on the chosen microcontroller, and the number of days available at the accredited certification laboratory inside the qualification window. Exhibit 4 shows the candidate features costed against all four resources rather than one.

The failure was not a bad ranking. It was a well-executed ranking against a non-binding constraint, which is the most expensive mistake in this topic precisely because it feels like competence all the way to the wall. The team had a roadmap, velocity, burn-down charts and predictable delivery. What it did not have was anyone asking which resource would run out first.

Recovery took three moves. First, a constraint register: a one-page list of every resource with a ceiling, its budget, its current consumption and its owner, reviewed monthly. Second, multi-constraint costing — every candidate feature costed against all four budgets before entering the backlog, which immediately killed F4's NB-IoT fallback at ₹ 190 a unit and 120 KB of flash and replaced it with a cheaper single-radio design. Third, and most importantly, the laboratory calendar was converted from a discovered constraint into a booked one: slots were reserved twelve weeks ahead and the software plan was built backwards from them. The general lesson is that hardware programmes make visible what software programmes hide. Software has exactly the same multiple constraints — infrastructure cost per transaction, a security review queue, a data-privacy assessment, an app-store review window — but because none of them appears in a sprint board, teams discover them one at a time, late.

8 Hard edge cases

Multi-product organisations and the internal market

When a platform team serves several products, each product computes its own shadow price and none of them can see the others'. Work then flows not to where value is highest but to whoever asks most persistently, which is an allocation mechanism with no relationship to value at all. Mature companies handle this with a quarterly capacity auction or an explicit internal price: each product is given an allocation of platform days and may trade it. Companies that say they do this and do not are recognisable by a platform roadmap that is a concatenation of whatever three product directors asked for, in the order they asked.

Two-sided marketplaces, where value is not additive

Chhanv Home Services, a marketplace matching households with electricians and plumbers across eleven cities, cannot maintain one prioritised list. The value of supply-side work — onboarding more electricians — depends entirely on whether demand in that city is unmet, and the value of demand-side work depends on whether supply can absorb it. In Pune the constraint may be supply and in Kochi demand, in the same week, which means the same item has a tenfold difference in density between two markets. The practice that works is to rank by constraint per market rather than per product, and to accept that the resulting plan is a portfolio of local decisions rather than a single global ordering. The failure mode is a national roadmap that optimises the average city, which exists nowhere.

Regulated products and the deadline cliff

Compliance work has a step-shaped cost of delay: near-zero value until a date, then catastrophic. A density model therefore ranks it last until it ranks first, and the transition is abrupt enough that it crowds out everything in the final quarter. Barve's e-way bill migration is a mild version; a payments company facing a regulatory deadline may lose an entire quarter of discretionary capacity. The mature practice is to book regulatory work into capacity the moment the date is published rather than the moment it becomes urgent, which converts a cliff into a smooth allocation. The immature practice — visible in any company that has a "compliance crunch" every year at the same time — is to let the arithmetic discover the cliff.

Hardware plus software

The Yantrika case is the general form. Physical products have several hard budgets — unit cost, mass, power, thermal envelope, certification calendar, tooling lead time — and they are coupled: relieving flash pressure by moving to a larger microcontroller consumes BOM headroom. The formal object is a multi-constraint knapsack, and the practical technique is to identify which budget is tightest as a ratio of demand to supply, solve against that, then check feasibility on the others. Crucially, some hardware constraints are irreversible in a way software constraints are not: a tooling order commits money that cannot be recovered by re-prioritising, so the option value of deferring a decision is a real term that density arithmetic does not contain.

AI-native products

Yograj AI Support, which resolves customer tickets for mid-market Indian companies, has a constraint set that would be unrecognisable to a traditional team. Engineering capacity is rarely binding. The binding resources are evaluation capacity — how many labelled examples the team can produce and review per week, which governs how fast any change can be validated — and inference cost per resolved ticket, which is a genuine unit-economic ceiling rather than a budget line. The deeper structural difference is that quality is stochastic and continuous: there is no clean boundary between a bug and a behaviour, because the model's error rate on a segment drifts rather than breaking. "A bug changed the ground" becomes "the error rate on refund queries rose from 4 per cent to 7 per cent over three weeks", which has a compounding cost-of-delay shape and no single ticket to prioritise. Teams that map this onto a defect workflow will consistently under-react.

What happens at the organisational seams

The recurring pathology across all of these is that shadow prices differ across boundaries and nobody computes both sides. Work gets pushed to whichever team has spare capacity rather than to where it is worth most; the constrained team is asked to be more efficient rather than given more people; and the elevation work that would fix it permanently sits at the bottom of a list, undervalued by construction. Barve's three-and-a-half-times gap is not unusual. It is what an organisation looks like when every team optimises its own list correctly.

9 Nine distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

The shadow price is the output; the list is a by-product

Competent practitioners produce a ranked plan. Experts produce a number — what one unit of the constrained resource is worth this cycle — and carry it into every subsequent conversation. The tell in the wild is how they answer "can we squeeze this in?". A competent PM says yes or no; an expert says "it costs nine days, and nine days is worth about ₹ 13 lakh at the margin, so tell me what it earns". The obvious reading, that this is pedantry, is wrong: it is the only mechanism that stops interrupts from being free, and the only one that makes a refusal defensible rather than territorial.

Utilisation is not scarcity

The busy team is not necessarily the constrained one. The constrained one is where finished work waits. Experts look for inventory — tickets in "ready for review", builds awaiting a device lab, designs awaiting sign-off — and treat a long queue as diagnostic evidence. The obvious reading is that everyone is busy so everyone is constrained; the reason it is wrong is that a non-bottleneck running at full utilisation simply builds up inventory in front of the bottleneck, which makes the system slower, not faster.

Density is computed against a constraint the model holds fixed

Every item whose purpose is to relax the constraint is undervalued by construction, because its return is denominated in released future capacity. Experts recognise this by a specific signature: an item that everybody agrees is obviously worth doing, that never rises above the line in three consecutive planning cycles, and that would reduce the team's own workload. The remedy is not a better score but a reserved envelope, because the value accrues outside the planning horizon the score covers.

The denominator is remaining effort, and slicing is a design act

Mid-cycle re-ordering uses work remaining, not work originally estimated; sunk days raise an item's density rather than obliging its completion. More subtly, the denominator is chosen, not observed. Experts attack the slice before the score, because a forty-five-day item that yields an eighteen-day slice worth sixty per cent of the value has just moved from below the line to near the top without anybody revising a single estimate. The tell is a team whose items are all large: they are not doing harder work, they are making their own constraint brutal.

Urgency, cost of delay and escalation are three different things

Escalation is a signal about a relationship. Urgency is a claim about a date. Cost of delay is a quantity with a shape. Experts ask the disambiguating question — what is different on the day after? — and find that perhaps a third of stated deadlines have no answer. The obvious reading is that this is a way of dismissing customers; in practice the opposite happens, because separating the three lets you take the real deadlines seriously enough to plan for them.

A defect's value is an avoided loss, and depends on the counterfactual

The escalating customer is a detection mechanism, not the affected population. The first question is how many others are hitting it, and the answer routinely changes the score by two orders of magnitude. The second question is whether the harm compounds: a cosmetic defect costs the same whenever you fix it, while a data-integrity defect creates a growing pool of corrupted records whose repair cost rises with delay. Experts separate reliability debt from defect count and refuse to let a bug backlog be managed by total volume.

Estimate error is asymmetric with size

Ratio ordering is robust to proportional estimation error — if everything is underestimated by thirty per cent, the order is unchanged — but not to correlated error, and error is strongly correlated with size. Large items are underestimated far more than small ones, which inflates exactly the densities that deserve most suspicion. The expert's routine is a sensitivity pass: multiply every large item by 1.6 and see whether the set above the line survives. The obvious reading is that better estimates would fix this; they would not, because the bias is cognitive rather than informational.

Greedy density starves the large strategic bet

Run a pure density fill for six consecutive quarters and the result is a roadmap of gravel: many small, high-density improvements and no repositioning of the product. This is not a failure of the arithmetic; it is the arithmetic working exactly as specified on a candidate set where big items always lose. The remedy is structural — a declared envelope, perhaps a fifth of capacity, that competes only within itself. The tell that a team needs one is a two-year history of shipping a great deal and changing nothing about its market position.

Confidence gets counted twice

Teams that discount value by a confidence factor and then also pad the effort estimate for risk have applied the same haircut twice, systematically demoting uncertain work below certain work by more than the evidence warrants. Experts pick one place for uncertainty and keep it there. The tell is a backlog in which every genuinely novel item — the ones that are uncertain precisely because nobody has done them — sits permanently below the line, while incremental work with confidence 1.0 fills the plan.

10 Where the field genuinely disagrees

Should escalations get a standing expedite lane?

The queueing argument for a reserved expedite lane is strong: holding fifteen to twenty per cent of the constrained resource free reduces variance in delivery for everything else, because a fully loaded system propagates every interrupt into every commitment. Against this, the organisational evidence is equally strong: a lane with a quota becomes an entitlement, sales teams learn its size, and within two quarters the lane is permanently full while the rest of the plan is untouched. Both positions rest on real evidence; the position you should hold depends on whether your organisation can keep a quota as a budget rather than converting it into a right. The test is whether anybody has ever been told the lane is full this month.

Should cost of delay be quantified for uncertain work?

The flow economist's steelman is that refusing to quantify does not avoid the estimate, it merely hides it — a decision was made, therefore a number was implied, and an implicit number cannot be argued with. The objector's steelman is that a fabricated figure acquires authority through arithmetic that its evidence does not support, and that for genuinely novel work the honest answer is a bet with an appetite rather than a valuation. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that quantified estimates for novel work outperform structured judgement, and the evidence for that is thin at best.

Fixed envelopes or item-by-item competition for debt and defects?

The envelope school — reserve, say, twenty per cent for technical debt and reliability — argues that this work systematically loses head-to-head against features because its benefits are diffuse and its costs are concrete. The competition school argues that envelopes become a protected budget inside which low-value work hides, and that the honest approach is to make debt work state its case in the same currency as everything else, which usually reveals that the top decile is far more valuable than any feature and the bottom half should never be done. Error budgets are the strongest synthesis available — they convert reliability into a quantity that automatically claims capacity when exceeded — but they only work where reliability is measurable, which excludes most of what is called technical debt.

Are estimates fit to serve as denominators at all?

The throughput school observes that teams with roughly consistent item sizes can forecast more accurately from historical throughput and item counts than from estimates, and that the effort spent estimating is itself a cost with no demonstrated return. The reply is that the denominator is doing two jobs: forecasting, where throughput may indeed be better, and pricing, where a per-item cost is needed to compare items against one another. Throughput has nothing to say about the second job. What would have to be true for the throughput school to be right about pricing is that item sizes are uniform enough for count to substitute for cost — occasionally true on mature platform teams, rarely elsewhere.

Is mid-cycle re-ordering ever net positive?

The stability school argues that within a short cycle the switching costs — lost context, aged partial work, damaged commitments — exceed almost any density gain available, so the correct policy is to freeze the cycle and queue everything for the next one. The responsiveness school replies that this is an argument for shorter cycles rather than for rigidity, and that a policy of never re-ordering is simply a policy of always paying whatever the interrupt costs. The disagreement is empirically resolvable within a given team by measuring completion rate against re-order frequency, and remarkably few teams have ever measured it.

11 What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in six observable ways. They ask what is displaced before they ask what is possible, which reverses the usual order of a planning conversation. They know the current shadow price of their team's constrained resource and quote it without looking it up. They hold a buffer and defend it as a decision rather than apologising for it as slack. They re-slice before they re-score, because the denominator is the variable they control. They maintain a written displacement log and send it to the people whose items moved, which makes the next refusal easier rather than harder. And they can tell instantly whether a given change requires a five-minute redraw or a genuine reconsideration, because they have classified what actually changed.

The negative signals are just as clear. Someone who has merely studied this will produce a RICE spreadsheet with three decimal places and no capacity number anywhere on it; will discuss the relative merits of six items after a single engineer goes on leave; will describe four items as P0; and will be unable to say, when asked, what last month's escalations pushed out. The spreadsheet is not the problem. The missing capacity number is.

12 What they decided

Barve made three moves and declined a fourth. He committed the ePOD workflow and the rate-engine optimisation to the quarter, pinned the e-way bill migration, and held fifteen days back as buffer — the plan in Exhibit 2. He then moved two core platform engineers onto the integrations squad for the remainder of the quarter, on the explicit argument that an engineer-day was worth ₹ 1.4 lakh there and ₹ 0.4 lakh where they had been, and used the additional ninety days to pull the self-serve carrier sandbox above the line on the elevated valuation of ₹ 3.5 lakh a day. He declined to promise Yashasvi Retail anything beyond ePOD, and sent the account team a written note saying which two items had been displaced and when they would return. What he did not do was hold a meeting to re-argue the value of the integrations backlog, because none of the three events had changed a single value estimate.

Deshpande hotfixed the crash on 17 February outside the release train; scoped the onboarding rebuild to a fourteen-day appetite and cut two screens to protect the 5 March train rather than protect the scope; deferred the pitch-detection improvement to April while escalating the five-week ML platform queue to her director as a capacity question rather than a priority question; and removed the subscription self-serve work from the discussion entirely. Her summary to the leadership team ran to four sentences and contained no ranked list at all, because on her problem the ranking was never the decision.

1. Barve's arbitrage across the seam was worth more than any re-ordering inside either list. Why had nobody computed the core platform's shadow price before, and what would an organisation have to change — in its planning artefacts, not its culture — for that number to exist by default?

2. The self-serve sandbox moved from ninth to fourth only once released capacity was valued at the squad's own shadow price. That valuation depends on the constraint persisting. Under what circumstances would the elevated number be self-defeating, and how would you know in advance?

3. Deshpande treated the crash as compounding and the retention work as linear. Suppose the compounding estimate of ₹ 3.4 lakh a day is wrong by a factor of three in either direction. Which of her four decisions changes — and what does your answer tell you about where analytical effort is actually worth spending?

13 Going deeper

RICE scoring is where the numerators in every exhibit on this page came from; constraints change the inputs to those scores rather than replacing them, so a PM who cannot defend a reach estimate cannot defend a plan built on it. Stakeholder mapping and management matters next because constraints do not arise spontaneously — they are imposed by people with interests, and knowing who can relax which one converts a fixed budget into a negotiable one. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing supply the denominator, which is where most of the error in any density calculation lives; the sensitivity pass described in section nine is unusable without it.

Saying no is the skill that makes the displacement statement survivable, turning an arithmetic result into a conversation the other person can accept. Allocating capacity across features, debt, bugs and bets is the structural remedy for greedy density's starvation of large work, and the place where the envelope-versus-competition disagreement in section ten is actually settled. Prioritising for hardware — cost, weight, power, schedule generalises the Yantrika failure into the multi-constraint case, which is the honest model even for pure software. Prioritising across conflicting stakeholders takes up what happens when two constituencies hold different value currencies and neither will convert.

Value versus effort is the two-by-two simplification of everything on this page, useful for speed and dangerous because it hides the capacity line. The Kano model supplies the missing idea that value is not linear in satisfaction, which explains why some low-density items are nevertheless non-negotiable. Weighted scoring and WSJF formalise the cost-of-delay-divided-by-duration rule and are the direct descendants of the flow-economics school. Buy-a-feature is the cleanest instrument for eliciting genuine trade-offs from customers, because it imposes a constraint on them rather than asking for preferences. User story mapping is the practical technique for producing the thin slices that section three insists on re-cutting. And strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation is the standing rebuttal from the strategy-first school: that the most valuable prioritisation decision is usually about which items reach the board at all, not which ones clear the line once they are there.
