Prioritising under constraints

When capacity, a customer or a bug changes the ground beneath a plan, the question is not which item is most valuable. It is which item now falls off the end — and what that displacement is worth.

1 A Thursday in Bengaluru

On the morning of Thursday 22 January 2026, Devika Menon had a plan that was eleven days old and two events away from being worthless. Menon was the product manager for the inventory squad at Yojak Systems, a Bengaluru company selling warehouse and order-management software to mid-market Indian retailers — about nine hundred paying accounts, roughly ₹ 58 crore of annual recurring revenue, five engineers on her squad and a six-week delivery cycle that had started on 12 January and would close on 6 March.

The first event arrived as a calendar invitation. Yojak's platform group had lost two engineers to a payments incident, and Menon's most experienced backend engineer was being seconded to them for three weeks. Fifteen planned engineer-days, gone, out of the hundred and twenty she had budgeted for the cycle.

The second arrived ninety minutes later as a support escalation. Chhavi Stores, an apparel chain running two hundred and forty outlets, had discovered that Yojak's goods-receipt module was writing duplicate entries into the stock ledger whenever a single receipt crossed about eight hundred line items. Their finance team had been reconciling by hand for nine days. Chhavi Stores was worth ₹ 2.1 crore a year to Yojak and its renewal date was 31 March. Yojak's support engineers had since found the same signature in the logs of roughly three hundred and sixty other high-volume accounts, none of whom had yet noticed.

By eleven o'clock Menon had four people in her inbox telling her what to do. Sales wanted the Chhavi Stores bug fixed today and the bulk goods-receipt import they had been promised kept in the cycle. The engineering manager wanted to know which item to stop. A second customer, Yatharth Wholesale, had a signed note in the account plan saying single sign-on would ship in this cycle. And the compliance lead wanted confirmation that the GST e-invoice schema update — mandated for a 1 April switchover — was still on track, because the next cycle would not close until 17 April.

None of these people were wrong. What Menon did in the next two hours would decide whether Yojak shipped a coherent cycle or four half-finished things, and whether the next escalation would arrive as a request or as a demand.

2 What the idea actually is

Prioritising under constraints means deriving an order of work from two separate things: a judgement about the value of each item, and a statement of the scarce resource that limits how many of them can happen. A constraint is anything that shrinks the set of plans you are able to execute — engineer-days in a cycle, a single shared design reviewer, a regulatory date, a hardware cost ceiling, a release train that departs once a fortnight. A prioritisation, properly speaking, is not a ranked list. It is a line drawn across a ranked list at the point where the constrained resource runs out.

The distinction matters because the two halves fail differently. A ranked list can be wrong because the value judgements are wrong. A plan can be wrong because the list was fine but the line was drawn in the wrong place, or because nobody noticed that the line had moved. Menon's Thursday is entirely a line problem. Nothing she believed about the value of single sign-on changed between Monday and Thursday. What changed was the amount of resource available, and the arrival of an item that had not previously existed.

The intellectual machinery is older than software. George Dantzig formalised linear programming at the US Air Force in 1947, and with it came the idea of a shadow price: for any binding constraint, the value of relaxing it by one unit. The knapsack problem — choosing which indivisible items to put in a bag of fixed capacity — gave the greedy rule that still governs most product backlogs: sort by value divided by the resource each item consumes, and fill from the top. Eliyahu Goldratt's The Goal (1984) added the organisational version, the Theory of Constraints: a system's output is set by its single tightest bottleneck, so improving anything else is theatre. Donald Reinertsen, in The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009), supplied the product-development vocabulary — cost of delay, and the sequencing rule of dividing it by duration. RICE, the scoring scheme most PMs meet first, was published by Intercom in 2016 and is best understood as one particular recipe for the numerator of that ratio, not as a theory of prioritisation in itself.

“We don't re-order because something got loud. We re-order because the constrained resource changed — and anything that comes in has to name what it pushes out.”

That is the sentence Menon can say in a room without sounding glib, because it is falsifiable. It commits her to two obligations: to identify what actually changed, and to publish the displacement rather than absorb it silently.

3 The mechanics, including the steps people leave out

The full procedure has seven steps. Most practitioners perform three of them and improvise the rest, which is why re-planning meetings run long.

First, name the constrained resource and check that it binds. A constraint binds if you would use more of it were it available. Engineer-days are the default assumption and frequently the wrong one: the true bottleneck is often a single specialist, a shared QA device lab, a security review queue, or a fortnightly release train. The diagnostic is not utilisation but waiting: where does finished work sit idle? At Yojak, engineer-days genuinely bind, because Menon has a queue of scoped work and no other blocked resource.

Second, separate what changed from what did not. Three kinds of event change the ground, and each touches a different part of the calculation. A capacity change moves only the budget line; it changes nothing about the value of any item, and re-arguing value after a capacity change is pure waste. A customer event changes the value estimate of specific items and may add a new constraint in the form of a promised date. A bug or incident does something subtler: it changes the state of the world, creating a cost that accrues for as long as you do not act, which means its value grows with delay while most feature value does not.

Third, pin the items that are not really items. Regulatory deadlines, contractual commitments and safety work are constraints wearing the costume of backlog entries. They come off the top of the capacity, before any ranking. Menon's GST e-invoice work is one of these: it scores badly on any value model and must ship anyway, because the cost of missing 1 April is not a lost benefit but a compliance breach.

Fourth, express value in a single currency and divide by effort. Whatever scheme produces the numerator — RICE, weighted scoring, a cost-of-delay estimate in rupees — the ordering rule is value per unit of the constrained resource, not value. This single division is the most commonly skipped step in the whole practice.

Fifth, fill until the resource runs out, and read off the price. The density of the first item that does not fit is the shadow price of the constraint: what one more unit of capacity is worth, and equally what one unit of interruption costs. This number, not the list, is the useful output.

Sixth, test the slicing before testing the ranking. The denominator is a design choice, not an observation. A forty-five-day item that does not fit may contain an eighteen-day slice that delivers most of the value. Re-slicing changes the ranking more often than re-scoring does.

Seventh, publish the displacement. Every addition names a subtraction, in writing, to the person who cares about the subtracted item. Absorbing an interrupt into unnamed slack is the single most corrosive habit in the discipline, because it teaches the organisation that interrupts are free.

4 The arithmetic, worked twice

Yojak scores value the way Intercom's RICE does: reach, the number of paying accounts materially touched in a quarter, multiplied by impact on a fixed scale (3 for massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low), multiplied by confidence as a fraction. The product is a dimensionless number the team calls value points. Effort is in engineer-days, from the squad's T-shirt sizing converted at S = 6, M = 12, L = 24 and XL = 45. Menon's cycle budget on 12 January was 120 engineer-days: five engineers, six weeks, thirty working days each, less twenty per cent for the support rota, interviews and leave.

Read the table slowly, because three things in it are easy to miss. The transfer API, D, is the most valuable single item at 945 points and is nearly last in the order, because it costs forty-five days. The invoice PDF redesign, C, is the least valuable item above the line at 180 points and is fourth, because it costs six. And the GST work, E, has the worst density on the board at 13 points per day and ships first, because density is irrelevant to items that are constraints rather than choices.

The most useful number is the one that never appears on a roadmap. The first item that does not fit is H, single sign-on, at 20 points per day. That is the shadow price of Menon's constraint: one engineer-day, in this cycle, buys about twenty points of value. Everything that happens on Thursday can now be priced in that currency instead of argued about.

The second pass, after Thursday

Two inputs move. Capacity falls from 120 to 105 engineer-days. And a new item, X, enters: the duplicate-ledger fix, scoped by the backend lead at nine days, with reach 360 accounts, impact 3 and confidence 1.0, because the defect is observed rather than hypothesised. Its value is 360 × 3 × 1.0 = 1,080 points, and its density is 1,080 ÷ 9 = 120 points per day — six times the shadow price. It is not a close call, and it is worth noticing why it is not close: bugs of this kind have very high density not because the benefit is enormous in the abstract but because the denominator is small and the confidence is 1.0.

Pinned work comes off first: E takes 20 days, leaving 85 discretionary. Then fill by density. X at 9 days leaves 76. F at 7 leaves 69. B at 12 leaves 57. A at 28 leaves 29. C at 6 leaves 23. Next in line is D at forty-five days, which does not fit — and here the greedy rule reaches its limit, because items are indivisible. The naïve response is to skip D and take G, which fits at fifteen days, leaving eight days idle and the squad's most valuable initiative untouched for six more weeks.

Menon's response was to attack the denominator instead. With the backend lead she split D into D1, a read-only transfer API sufficient for the three customers who had asked, at eighteen days and 520 points — a density of 28.9 — and D2, the write path and reconciliation, at twenty-seven days and the residual 425 points, a density of 15.7. D1 fits in the remaining twenty-three days with five to spare. Note what the split did: it moved part of D from below the line to well above it, higher than both C and E. Re-slicing changed the ranking without a single value estimate being revised.

The shadow price also lets Menon price the two events rather than apologise for them. The escalation consumed nine days at twenty points a day, so it cost about 180 points of displaced value and bought 1,080 — a trade she can defend in one line. The secondment cost fifteen days at twenty points a day, roughly 300 points, which is very nearly the entire value of the single sign-on project. That is the number she takes to the engineering director: not “we are under pressure”, but “three weeks of one engineer cost this cycle about the value of the SSO release”.

5 Seven distinctions that separate understanding from vocabulary

Ranking is not allocation

A prioritised backlog is an ordering; a plan is an ordering plus a line. People who have only the first will tell you an item is “high priority” and be genuinely surprised when it does not ship, because in their mental model priority is a property of the item rather than a relationship between the item and a budget. The tell is a roadmap with no capacity number on it anywhere. Ask what the team's capacity is in whatever unit the estimates use; if nobody can say, no prioritisation is occurring, only sorting.

Density, not value

The greedy rule is value divided by the constrained resource, and the rule is exactly correct only when items are divisible. When they are not — and features rarely are — greedy density is a very good heuristic that occasionally strands capacity, as it nearly did with D. The routine error is to rank by value alone, which pushes large items to the top and quietly guarantees that a cycle produces one unfinished epic. The diagnostic takes ninety seconds: recompute the list by value per day and see whether the top five changes. If it changes a lot, the team has been ranking by value.

The denominator is remaining effort, not original effort

When re-ordering mid-cycle, the effort figure that belongs in the division is what is left to do, not what the item originally cost. Ten days already spent on D are sunk; they raise D's density for the remainder of the cycle rather than obliging anyone to finish it. This is the one place where the accountant's instinct and the prioritiser's instinct genuinely agree, and it is still the place where teams most often talk themselves into finishing something because of what it has already cost.

Urgency is not cost of delay

An escalation raises the volume; it does not necessarily raise the value. The question that separates the two is: what is different on the day after the date? For the GST switchover, the answer is that Yojak's customers cannot file compliant invoices — a step change, a real deadline. For a customer who wants something “by end of month”, the answer is frequently that nothing at all is different, which means there is no deadline, only a preference with a date attached.

A bug's value is an avoided loss, and it depends on the counterfactual

X scored 1,080 because 360 accounts are affected, not because Chhavi Stores is angry. Had the defect been genuinely unique to one customer's configuration, its reach would have been 1, its value about 3, and its density a third of a point per day — below everything on the board, and correctly so. The escalating customer is a detection mechanism, not the population. Experts always ask how many others are affected before scoring the fix, and the answer frequently changes the decision by two orders of magnitude.

The binding constraint is often not engineer-days

Yojak's constraint was engineering capacity because the work was scoped and the design was done. Change either of those and the bottleneck moves: if one designer serves three squads, design is the constraint and adding engineers makes queues longer, not shorter. The diagnostic is to look for finished work waiting: tickets sitting in “ready for review”, builds waiting on a shared device lab, releases waiting for a fortnightly train. Prioritising the non-binding resource is the most expensive form of busywork in product management, because it feels exactly like doing the job.

What the method cannot tell you

Density arithmetic ranks the items you thought of. It has nothing to say about whether the right items are on the board, whether the strategy is sound, or whether the value numbers mean anything. It also has a structural bias that every serious practitioner must counter deliberately: small cheap items have high density, so a pure greedy fill will, quarter after quarter, produce a roadmap of gravel and never the one large bet that changes the company's position. The standard remedy is an envelope — a fixed share of capacity reserved for strategic work and competed within itself, never against the gravel.

6 How this changes with product type and company size

In consumer products, reach is large and estimated from funnel data, so numerators are statistical rather than negotiated, and the binding constraint is often not engineering at all but experiment slots: a team can only run so many A/B tests on the same surface before the results become uninterpretable. Prioritisation there is frequently a question of which hypothesis occupies the surface, and the shadow price is denominated in experiment-weeks.

In B2B, constraints arrive with names attached. Reach is small and lumpy — Yatharth Wholesale is sixty accounts' worth of revenue in one logo — and commitments made in a sales cycle become constraints that outrank density, because credibility is an asset that a renewal conversation prices. The mature B2B habit is to reserve a declared slice of every cycle for commitment work, so that the promise is made against a budget rather than against optimism.

In marketplaces the complication is that value is jointly produced by two sides, so an item's numerator depends on the state of the other side. Onboarding a thousand new service providers has enormous value when demand is unmet in a city and close to zero when it is not; the same item's density can swing tenfold between two cities in the same week. The practical consequence is that marketplace teams cannot maintain one global ranking. They rank by constraint per market — supply-constrained cities get one order, demand-constrained cities another.

Company stage changes the cost of re-ordering more than the arithmetic. In a thirty-person company, re-ordering is cheap: few dependencies, no external commitments, and the value of responding to new information exceeds the value of stability, so weekly re-planning is rational. In a two-thousand-person company, a single re-order propagates into marketing calendars, partner integrations, support training and sales commitments, and the cost of the change frequently exceeds the density gain it captures. That is why large firms hold quarterly planning and pre-commit capacity envelopes: not because they are slow, but because their switching costs are genuinely higher. A PM who moves from one to the other and keeps the old cadence will be described, accurately, as either chaotic or sclerotic.

7 Four common mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

Silent absorption

The symptom, visible from outside, is that commitments slip without anyone ever having decided to slip them: the cycle review lists four of seven items shipped and the explanation is “we had a lot of interrupts”. The misunderstanding is that unnamed slack can absorb new work. It cannot; it can only hide the displacement until the last day. The diagnostic is to ask what was displaced by last month's three escalations. If nobody can name the displaced items, the team is absorbing rather than deciding, and the organisation has learned that interrupts are free.

Re-litigating value when only capacity moved

The symptom is a ninety-minute meeting after an engineer goes on leave, in which the relative merits of six items are argued from first principles. The misunderstanding is that all changes are alike. A capacity change moves the line and nothing else; the correct response is a five-minute redraw. The diagnostic is a single question at the top of the meeting — which input actually changed? — and if the answer is “capacity”, the value discussion is closed by rule.

Escalation-ordered backlogs

The symptom is that the order of work correlates almost perfectly with the seniority of whoever last complained, and the roadmap changes every week. The misunderstanding is that responsiveness and prioritisation are the same virtue. The diagnostic is to score the last five expedited items after the fact using the team's own model and compare their densities with the items they displaced. In teams with this problem, roughly half the expedites score below what they pushed out, which converts an argument about culture into an argument about arithmetic.

Estimate theatre

The symptom is elaborate precision in the numerator — reach estimated to three significant figures — paired with denominators that are a year old and a team that has never checked whether L-sized items really take twenty-four days. The misunderstanding is that accuracy lives in the value model. It usually lives in the effort model, because effort error is systematically biased: large items are under-estimated far more than small ones, which inflates exactly the densities that should be treated with most suspicion. The diagnostic is a sensitivity test — multiply every L and XL estimate by 1.6 and see whether the order above the line changes. If it does, the plan is resting on the estimates, not on the values.

8 What good looks like

Handled well, Menon's Thursday takes about ninety minutes and produces four artefacts. There is a one-line statement of what changed: fifteen engineer-days lost, one new defect affecting 360 accounts. There is a recomputed table with a line drawn on it and a shadow price written at the bottom. There is a displacement note sent to three named people — the Yatharth Wholesale account manager, the operations lead who wanted the returns report, and the platform group waiting on the transfer API — each saying what moved, to when, and why, in the same currency. And there is one sentence in the cycle log recording that five days were held back as buffer, so that the next interrupt has somewhere to land.

What is conspicuously absent is a debate about whether single sign-on matters. It does. It lost on density to items that matter less in total but cost far less per day, and it will win in the next cycle when it starts with a full budget in front of it. Good prioritisation under constraint is unemotional in exactly this way: it makes the losses explicit and small rather than implicit and cumulative.

9 What Menon decided

She shipped the plan in Exhibit 2. The duplicate-ledger fix went in immediately and was released to all affected accounts within four days, which meant Chhavi Stores got a fix and three hundred and sixty other customers got one before they knew they needed it — the part of the decision that the escalation itself would never have produced. The GST work stayed pinned. The transfer API went in as a read-only slice, which gave the three customers asking for it something real while leaving the write path for March. Single sign-on moved out, in writing, with a date in the next cycle and a note to the account team explaining that it had lost by twenty points a day and would start the next cycle at the top of the discretionary list.

The reasoning is worth stating plainly, because it is the whole topic in one paragraph. Menon did not decide what was most important. She decided what her constrained resource could buy, priced the two events that had consumed part of it, and published the consequences to the people who would otherwise have discovered them at the end of the cycle.

What to learn next follows directly from what this page could not do. The value numbers came from somewhere, and RICE scoring is where to interrogate them, since constraints change the inputs to those scores rather than replacing them. The denominators came from engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing, which is the constraint's currency and therefore the place where most of the error lives. The constraints themselves came from people, which makes stakeholder mapping the study of where they originate. And the displacement note Menon sent is the beginning of saying no — the skill of making a refusal legible, priced and survivable.

1. Menon's shadow price of twenty points per engineer-day makes interruption priceable. What would change in her organisation's behaviour if that number were published every cycle — and who would resist publishing it?

2. The duplicate-ledger fix scored 1,080 because 360 accounts were affected. Suppose the investigation had found only Chhavi Stores affected, making the fix score three points. Would you still have shipped it in this cycle, and if so, on what basis — given that the basis cannot be the arithmetic?
